speechtext: The question of the Highlander and the Britisher, as the hon. gentleman has remarked, was up a few days ago on a question by the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Quinn). I wish to say that at that time I gave to the house a statement which was given to me by Mr. Fullerton and which I presume was given to him by the steamship management under him, which statement I believe has since been shown to be somewhat inaccurate. In other words, my understanding to-day is that as regards the questions asked by the hon. gentleman, the answer to that regarding the second boat, the Britisher, is: Yes, an inquiry was made of the Saint John dry dock, to see if it could accept that ship; but in regard to the other, I am informed more or less authoritatively that such inquiry was not made. Since there was some question as to the truth of the statement, which I made here, of course on the authority of the management who are entirely in control, I informed Mr. Fullerton that the government desired a complete investigation into the whole question. We insisted that as far as possible all ships of the Canadian fleet must be repaired in Canadian shipyards, even if sometimes that makes it necessary to repair them in advance of the regular time. The investigation is now going on, and as the matter is in a sense sub judice I do not think I should say anything further at present.

Wheat Quotas
On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. HANSON (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speechtext:
On Monday evening last the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot), and I think also the hon. member for Willow Bunch (Mr. Donnelly) put a question to me when the estimates of the Department of Trade and Commerce were under discussion, with reference to Canada having loaned part of her so-called quota to Argentina. These questions are found on pages 2070 and 2081 of Hansard.
I desire to say that no part of the Canadian wheat export quota for the crop year 1933-34 or for the crop year 1934-35 was in fact transferred or loaned to Argentina. If the statement made in the House of Commons on May 11, 1934, by the Prime Minister, to which the hon. member for Temiscouata referred, is read carefully it will be seen that what the Prime Minister actually said was:
Any concessions that might be made to the Argentine by reason of the extraordinarily large crop they had would not involve Canada in the loss of any shipments that we might be able to make, for the quota we had for the year was a quota that was greater than we should be able to fill under existing probabilities. In any event it would be merely a loan of a part of our quota until next year, so that we would not lose anything if we made an adjustment with the Argentine.
The Prime Minister was referring to conversations then in progress during which the other overseas wheat exporting countries had expressed their willingness, subject to certain safeguarding conditions, to transfer temporarily to Argentina part of their export quotas that were unlikely to be used. In the event, Argentina was not willing to subscribe to the safeguarding conditions, and so no transfer of quota from Canada to Argentina ever took place. There is therefore no question of Argentina returning something which that country never received.

the house, unless the Speaker finds that throughout the procedure everything has been in order-an almost impossible situation.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. J. MANION (Minister of Railways) :
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I should like at once to congratulate my colleague the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) on the clear, frank and very able statement which he has given of conditions not only in Canada but in the world at large, so far as business affairs are concerned, and I congratulate him as well upon the fearless yet fair application of taxes to those best able to bear them. Since the presentation of the budget the press of Canada has been very generous in its praise; in fact, the approval of the budget has been so general that,

The Budget-Mr. Manion
it seems to me, rarely has such unanimity been in evidence, in all the years that I have been a member of this house, as there has been on this occasion in connection with the present budget; and probably the best compliment which was paid the Minister of Finance was in the more or less unanimous nickname, if I may so describe it, which was given the budget when it was called "the poor man's budget." I believe it is a poor man's budget inasmuch as it goes further than we have yet gone in this country in the redistribution of wealth and in placing taxes where they should be placed-

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: On the poor man.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In this budget there are no taxes on the poor -man, but they are placed on those who are well able to bear them.
I have listened, as I always do, with a great deal of interest, to my hon. friend from Shel-burne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston), the official financial critic of the opposition. In a speech which took two hours and forty minutes, the hon. gentleman I must confess almost rivalled his leader in the length of the addresses which that right hon. gentleman gives, and he still maintains that air of pessimism and defeatism which he displayed last year and the year before, in spite of the fact that so far as Canada is concerned-and I think so far as the world generally is concerned-the corner has been turned in regard to the depression. In fact it was turned well over a year ago, but my hon. friend, or I think I should say my hon. friends opposite, find no gratification in that. There is no pleasing them with anything. I am sorry for them; they cannot cheer up. The hon. gentleman in his usual eloquent manner wept, wailed and gnashed his teeth about the terrible conditions in Canada. I believe he did endeavour on one or two occasions to say that he was very glad conditions were getting better, but he proceeded immediately to show that they were getting worse. As I listened to him-and I did attentively-I decided that there could be a very good biblical description of his speech: it was a strange mixture of the wailings of Jeremiah, the doubtings of Thomas, and a few dashes of the flavouring of Ananias. My hon. friend is being affected I think by the fact that he does not remain in his own province. He comes I am told from a very charming constituency, that of Shelburne-Yarmouth, a constituency that juts out into the broad Atlantic where the tang -of the salt air comes in and keeps the cobwebs out of people's brains. Yet the hon. gentleman has come up to live on St. James Street where budgets are always unpopular, because the
moguls down there, before the budget comes out, fear they may be taxed, and after it comes out, they usually find they have been. Consequently I am afraid my hon. friend is being affected by them. I would suggest to him with all due respect and the utmost friendliness that he go back and spend more of his time in his constituency, in which event he would probably not only be sure of reelection, -but would also clear out from his brain those cobwebs of depression.
I notice that the opposition seem to be in this mood: if the general depression continued to lead the people of Canada down into the valleys, they would be happy, because then they would- be able to float on the tide of discontent that is present always in crises of this nature, once more back into power. But as they see business picking up in this country and conditions improving throughout the world, they feel that hope of victory which they did possess a year ago, and I think with some just cause owing to conditions, is gradually -being banished from their minds and they are getting more and more afraid that we shall perhaps hold the election off until much better conditions have finally arrived and the people can judge normally as they should, and return to power an administration which has given Canada such splendid government.
The Liberal motto seems to be not "country first," but "party and politics first"; that is their attitude. There is no acknowledgment of world conditions, no acknowledgment of a crisis that was more severe than the world has seen in its economic history, a crisis in which two-thirds of the world trade was wiped out altogether, in which tens of millions of people in the industrial countries were unemployed, in which economic nationalism has been rampant throughout the world, in which dictatorships have sprung up in half the countries of Europe, and in which repudiation of interest and even of debt has become quite common. In a time when the maintenance of the democratic institutions in which we believe is an achievement, my hon. friends opposite talk as if conditions in the world were all normal. May I ask them this question: What country or what people escaped the world depression? The answer is obvious: No country and no people. My hon. friends opposite have a habit-and my hon. friend exhibited it in his speech-of showing business conditions in Canada between, say 1926 and 1929, and trying to take the credit for them. All they were doing at that time was floating forward on a wave of the wildest kind of boom, and if they must get the credit for that, then they must also take the blame for the depression which followed and for all the
The Budget-Mr. Manion

tragedy that succeeded upon, the depression of 1929. To the Liberals, apparently, at any rate to the Liberals in the house, it seems to be no achievement that Canada came through at least as well as if not better than did any other country. They set off on a smug pretence of cooperation with and assistance to this government, when as a matter of fact all we have received from them in the five years during which we have been in power, has been criticism, fault-finding, and every possible attempt at embarrassment that they could think of. They have become the party of reaction, of stand-patism, of laissez-faire. Apparently those are their principles at the present time.
Even if I wanted to, I could not for lack of time go into every detail of the speech of the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth, because he spoke for two hours and forty minutes and I have not that time at my disposal. But if I had the time I could do this: I think I could take almost every positive statement that the hon. gentleman made and show that in most or practically all of the cases he twisted the facts to suit his own purpose, or if he did not do that, he did as at least some lawyers have such an ability to do; he twisted the argument in such a way as to deprecate the achievements of the government. The hon. gentleman has now a habit, which he has practised at least since he has been in opposition, of keeping always down in the valleys. He seems to forget that sometimes the sun is shining on the hill tops. He keeps on dealing with small matters when, with his natural ability, he could be on the hill tops dealing with the bigger questions, and he could deal with them very ably.
I am going to discuss a few of his statements and show what I mean by saying that most of them could be disproved. For example he stated that the Minister of Finance had spoken of the wiping out of trade restrictions only as a preelection discovery. I had on my desk in my room the budget speeches for the past two years, 1933 and 1934. but apparently I forgot to bring them down with me. I meant to quote the 1933 one, that is two years ago, in which the Minister of Finance very clearly pointed out to the people of this country that there was too much economic nationalism; that tariffs were too high throughout the world; that no individual country could lower its tariffs, but that all countries should wipe out so far as they could the economic nationalism which was swamping world trade. He pointed that out in 1933 and again in 1934.
Then the hon. gentleman belittled the tariff changes in the budget. Last year, as I re-

Now just a word in regard to balancing the budget. The hon. gentleman criticized the Minister of Finance very severely because he was not balancing the budget, and he also criticized us because during our regime we have added to the public debt. I should like to ask him or any hon. member who speaks what country has balanced its budget during these trying times. I do not know any country of any importance that has done so. Let us take France, for example, one of the richest countries in the world. The other day I read a statement, which I hold in my hand, made by the Minister of Finance of that country. It is dated at Paris, and according to this statement France has to borrow $1,326,000,000 in order to balance its budget. The statement is as follows:
Paris, January 23.-France must borrow approximately 21,000.000,000 francs (about $1,326,000,000) in 1935 to balance its budget

The Budget-Mr. Manion
and prime its economic pump, Louis Germain-Martin, finance minister, told the finance committee to-day. The money so raised would be in addition to !the budget income estimated at 46,991,000,000 francs (about $3,101,406,000).
Just in passing I should like to mention that the $3,000,000,000 which France collects in taxes is nearly ten times the amount we collect in Canada, but France's population is not four times the population of Canada. In other words they collect in taxes about twice as much per head as we do in Canada.
Then there is England. In my address on the budget last year I pointed out that England is not balancing its budget, because England is not paying interest on its war debt to the United States, which amounts to nearly S200,000,000. If we did not pay the interest on our war debt we would not find very great difficulty in balancing our budget, because in round figures the annual interest on our war debt amounts to $100,000,000. For fear someone may say that I am incorrectly stating the facts I am going to quote a few words from the budget speech of 1934 of Mr. Neville Chamberlain, Chancellor of the Exchequer in England:
Neither last year nor the year before did I make any provision for the payment of the war debt to America nor for the receipt of war debts or reparations by ourselves. In the absence of any future development, I propose to follow precisely the same line this year.
Again I should like to point out that the taxes collected in England amount to half a billion dollars more than the taxes collected in France, or about $3,500,000,000, which works out at about $90 per head while our taxes in Canada to-day, even if you include provincial taxes, amount to about $45 per head. So if we in Canada imposed taxes on the same basis as they are imposed in England, instead of having a deficit we would have $300,000,000 or $400,000,000 with which we would not know what to do.
Then let us look at the situation in the United States. This year that country has a deficit of between $4,000,000,000 and $5,000,000,000. I hold in my hand a statement from a financial paper, either the Wall Street Journal or Barron's Weekly, I think the Wall Street Journal, of a few weeks ago showing that they expect a deficit of $4,500,000,000 in the United States. That works out at about forty times our deficit, though their population is only about twelve times the population of Canada. So on a basis of population their deficit is about three times as great as the. deficit of the Dominion of Canada.
It is true that we have a deficit quite large enough; if you include everything it amounts to about $117,000,000, and the Minister of
Finance admitted an increase in the public debt of $670,000,000 since we came into power, though he claimed that part of that sum should be charged to the late government, and I think he was right. However, we will take it as $670,000,000. That is a very serious addition to the public debt and I am not going to belittle it, but at the same time I would point out that if the war had continued for another year we would have added almost that amount to our public debt, but we would not have closed our doors; we would not have pulled down our blinds and quit the war. I submit again, and with all seriousness, that while our public debt is quite serious enough it would be diminished very quickly with a reasonable revival of world trade, not only Canadian trade but world trade. During that period we would be able to take into this country, as we can take in during normal times, a proper proportion of immigrants, and as we get a larger population our problems will vanish like mists before the rising sun. We have this advantage over European countries, that we have great vacant spaces, and when world trade picks up and the world becomes normal again, we will fill those vacant spaces. So, sir, I submit that this is not a time to paint our picture darker than it really is; it is a time for optimism, not a time for blue ruin.
The hon. gentleman said that by increasing our trade we could not only balance our budget but solve our railway problem. He said we were strangling trade, though I noticed he was not so emphatic in that regard this year as he was last year, doubtless because we have increased the total trade of Canada in the past year, as compared with 1932, by something over $300,000,000. Trade has been strangled throughout the world because of the economic nationalism and the self sufficiency that has been desired by the countries of the world in case of another war. I submit, sir, in all sincerity, and I am sure my hon. friends cannot deny it, that ten million people in the Dominion of Canada are not sufficiently powerful to control world trade. Did the Liberals control it when they were in power? One must ask that question. The hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth spoke of the railway question. Now if there is any group in this country which should hesitate to talk about the railway question it is the group directly opposite, because they
handed over to this government a railway mess the like of which Canada never had before, although we have had some messes. The hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth again brought up that old chestnut that he pulls off every time he speaks, that the Liberal party during their regime saved the people of this country on the national debt $257,000,000. But he always forgets the other half of the story; I pointed it out over and over again and I am going to point it out again to-day because it should be known. The other half, or the other three-quarters of the story is that while the Liberal government were saving on the national debt, they were adding to the railway debt by $461,000,000 during the time they were in power. In other words, the net addition to the public debt for which they were directly and indirectly responsible is well over $200,000,000, and so it is no wonder that I jocularly added Ananias to the other biblical characters I mentioned in describing the hon. gentleman's speech. I have in my hand a sheet showing the interest, payments due by the Canadian National Railways from the years of their incorporation down to the present time, and I intend to refer briefly merely to the time when my hon. friends opposite were in power.
In 1921 the interest owing to the public was $35,000,000 in round figures. When hon. gentlemen went out of power in 1930 the interest owing to the public was exactly $51,000,000. In the following year, due to the expenditures they made, it was $55,000,000, nearly $56,000,000. So between the time they came into power and the time they went out of power the interest owing to the bondholders of the Canadian National Railways was increased by over $20,000,000 for which hon. gentlemen opposite were entirely responsible due to the heavy capital expenditures which they made. The funded debt was increased by $461,000,000 and the interest charges by over $20,000,000.
But that is not all, because there was the government debt as well. The interest owing to the government in 1921 was $20,000,000, and that had increased in the year hon. gentlemen opposite went out of power to $32,000,000. If you add the two increases together it means increased interest charges during the regime of hon. gentlemen opposite of $32,000,000. It is true that so far as the interest due to the government of $12,000,000 is concerned it was not paid, and probably never will be, but those figures show the great increases which my hon. friends opposite made in capital expenditures.
There was another boast which the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth brought up
The Budget-Mr. Manion

last year and again this year about the national railways. He said that during the years the Liberals were in power the railways had earned an average of $24,000,000 above operating expenses. I will admit that that is correct. But my hon. friend always forgets the other half of that story as well, and that is that though the railways earned an average of $24,000,000 above operating expenses they were still down, at the end of the nine years my hon. friends opposite were in power, $140,000,000 on interest account to the bondholders. In other words, in those nine years the railways were short of paying interest by $140,000,000. I mention this because the facts should be kept straight. I do not think that half truths of that sort should go out to confuse the people of this country.
My hon. friend used a phrase that has been used very often in this house and elsewhere. He said that the Canadian National Railways were a "conglomeration of junk railways" when taken over.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And my hon. friend from Sherbrooke says hear, hear.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: When taken over.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I will put up against the hon. gentlemen a gentleman whom they praised very highly and whom they boasted of having brought to this country, and that is Sir Henry Thornton. He was appointed in October, 1922, and after he had made an inspection with the boards of directors of the Canadian National Railways of the roads he said in his report of 1923:
On behalf of the board I would like to state that after inspection-
Get that-after inspection:
-of the main arteries of the system we find that the three groups of lines, until recently the Canadian National Railways, entered the consolidation in excellent physical condition and operating at a high mark of efficiency as regards actual performance or movement of traffic and other factors controllable by management.
On some of the older sections there are still improvements that should be undertaken but in the main the lines are modern in character and were built or have been brought up to standards which are ahead of actual traffic requirements, except under stress of seasonal movements.
I will leave that statement without discussing it any further. My hon. friend quoted me as having made this statement at Inger-soll-that the mess which this country got into in the early years of this century, in consequence of the building of too many railways-two other transcontinental lines where one would have sufficed-must be ascribed to

both the old parties; he said that I declared at Ingersoll that probably the old parties deserved blame to the extent of fifty-fifty. I do not withdraw that statement. I think that probably the whole populace of Canada in the early days of the century were insanely optimistic, and though the building of railways on this scale really started under the Liberals-in 1904 when the Transcontinental was under discussion, and again in 1908 when there was further talk about the other transcontinental-I say that everyone must share in the responsibility. I accept the statement which I am supposed to have made at Ingersoll; I do not remember having made it, but I neither withdraw nor deny it. At the moment however I am not dealing with the past history of the railway problem in Canada. What I complain about is this, that during the time when my hon. friends opposite had these railways in trust for the people of Canada, expenditures were made which I submit should not have been undertaken, and that is what I criticize. In the pre-election year, 1929, I pointed out that they had spent money, or perhaps had forced the Canadian National Railways to spend money to a scandalous degree. They either permitted or forced the Canadian National to spend money on this scale-I do not know which term to use, though I am sure that no sane railway men would have allowed themselves willingly to spend as was done in 1929. At any rate, my hon. friends, if they did not force the railways, allowed the management of the Canadian National Railway System in 1929, one year before the election, to add to the debt of this country the huge sum of anywhere from $200,000,000 to $250,000,000 to be spent o>n hotels, terminals, passenger ships, which are rotting at the docks, branch lines and purchases of all kinds of old lines which have never paid their way. They added 810,000,000 a year to the annual interest payments of the Canadian National Railways. I do not suggest that all this sum, between S200,000,000 and $250,000,000, was wasted, but I do contend that very much of it was. I say that most of it was of no use to the Canadian National Railways, and it did not serve any purpose so far as the employees themselves were concerned. It merely added annual charges to the Canadian National Railways, and in respect of a branch of service which has always been losing money-that is, the passenger services. The passenger services of the Canadian National Railways lost, in the year 1926, the huge sum, on operating, of $4,000,000, and every year after that until 1931, a period of five years, the losses have

The Budget-Mr. Manion
mounted up in gradual progression until they reached in 1931 the sum of $24,000,000 on account of operating. And yet it was upon these passenger services-steamships, Montreal terminus, hotels, radio and things of that sort-it was upon these services, a losing branch of the system, that these huge sums were spent. Then I will refer to one sentence in the report of the royal commission on railways. They contrasted the construction costs of branch lines built by the Canadian Pacific Railway and by the Canadian National Railways in the years between 1923 and 1931 inclusive, because those were the years of new management and of consolidation of the railways, and they found that the Canadian National had a total excess cost of over $30,000,000 on 1,895 miles of construction. That was during my hon. friends' regime, and what I submit to you, Mr. Speaker, is this. They were the trustees of the Canadian people with respect to these railways; they were in charge of the system for the people of Canada, and they should have maintained a greater control over the management than they did. They should have insisted upon a board of directors who would not be merely rubber stamps; they should have seen to it that the management prevented such a condition of affairs from developing.
Well, we cleaned up that mess, and I say now to the credit of the Canadian National Railways that we have to-day an efficient and economically managed railway system. Some of the figures in regard to gross earnings will prove this statement, because if we can get back to $250,000,000-and in the last ten or fifteen years we have had around $250,000,000 gross earnings in about half of them-the railways would be very close to the position where they would pay interest on their debt to the public. At any rate, the system would be so close to that position that the people of Canada could easily absorb the balance and take care of it as an investment on behalf of the development of the country generally.
But in spite of the results which we have obtained in economical and efficient management of the Canadian National Railways, there are still insidious rumours abroad, a whispering compaign against this government, to the effect that we are out for amalgamation. There are stories of unfair treatment of the Canadian National Railways on our part; there are tales of our favouring the Canadian Pacific Railway. It is a whispering campaign of the most vicious sort. I brand it to-day as a whispering campaign of the most vicious sort, and I will give proof for that statement, because these rumours reach me as Minister 92582-137
of Railways. They come from all parts of the country. For example, on March 22, five days ago, a Colonel Streight, a Liberal candidate in one of the Toronto constituencies, is reported as follows in the Toronto Star:
Score rail merger at Liberal meet.
If Bennett plans allowed 75,000 men will be jobless.
Denouncing any merger of Canada's railways, Colonel J. E. L. Streight, Liberal standard-bearer in West York federal riding, last night promised the Humbercrest and South Runny-mede Liberal Association a Liberal government would not permit such an amalgamation.
Plans are already being made by the Bennett government to complete the merger,-
May I say that this is just a plain, ordinary, everyday falsehood.
-if returned to power, he told his audience, largely composed of railwaymen, and declared if such a move is permitted 75,000 railroad workers will be thrown out of employment. The Canadian Pacific Railway has already been advanced $60,000,000 without interest, he said.
The Canadian Pacific Railway has not been advanced any part of the $60,000,000 by this government. The government guaranteed it, but that is a small matter-

speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Well, it is a small matter compared to these vicious charges based on falsehood. This gentleman may be straight in name but he is crooked in his political methods. As the Minister of Public Works points out, we have good security for the guarantee of the $60,000,000.
With respect to these rumours which are afloat against this government, most unfair and vicious rumours of all kinds, let me say that there has been no thought on the part of this government of bringing about amalgamation of the two railways. No one on this side of the house, either in the front lines or in the rear, so far as I know, has come out for the amalgamation of the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Pacific Railway. My right hon. leader (Mr. Bennett) in Winnipeg used a phrase which has since been quoted and which he has never gone back on-Competition ever, amalgamation never. This government is not favourable to amalgamation. In the Canadian National-Canadian Pacific railway bill of 1933 we incorporated clause 27 which forbids amalgamation. Yet certain people-I do not say my hon. friends opposite, because they are too honourable, but some of their friends-continue to spread rumours and tales of this kind, vicious stories not based on the truth. The only man in this house who has come out openly for amalgamation is the hon.

The Budget-Mr. Manion

member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler). He called it unification, but that to my mind is another name for the same thing.
I repeat here, what I said at Brockvilie and at Smiths Falls, that under present conditions there is no solution for the Canadian railway problem by means of amalgamation. The only possible solution for the railway situation in this country is a revival of world business and world trade, and we have no control over that. I repeat, a country with a population of ten millions cannot control world trade, and to my mind this country cannot continue paying its debts without a revival in world business and world trade. Personally I think world business and trade are going to continue on the upward trend as they have been doing for more than a year past. All the railways on this continent have been hit by the depression. Many railways in the United States have gone into bankruptcy and more of them would have done so if they had not been helped by the United States government. But I repeat there is no cure for the railway question if by cure or solution you mean the payment of all the interest owing to the public through any such idea as unification or amalgamation, and I would point out that a united railway made up of the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National would make a huge monopoly in this country with, say in round figures, 175,000 employees who with their friends and relations would have a voting power of something like 300,000 people, in addition to which there would be the power of a huge system such as that in its purchases and other methods of getting support. I have never said this before, but I say it to-day: To my mind such a huge monopoly as that would be a menace to the political and economic life of this nation; that is my feeling about the matter. It would also bring about political and public pressure so severe, as spoken of in the Duff report, that probably no government could live under it. I do not intend to deal further to-day with the question of amalgamation, but I want it clearly understood that this government is not for amalgamation, has never come out for it, and anybody who makes statements to that effect wilfully tells what is not true. I have tried to make that as clear as I can.

Certainly; the government includes the Prime Minister, and I am speaking for the government and the Prime Minister if the hon. member wants them enumerated separately.
Another matter in regard to the railways which the hon. member for Shelburne-Yar-mouth mentioned, was the question of arbitral tribunals. He was most unfair in his statement; he said that there would have been arbitral tribunals set up if we had appointed a chairman of the board of railway commissioners. I make the statement that neither President Beatty of the Canadian Pacific nor Chairman Fullerton of the Canadian National nor anybody else representing them has directly or indirectly ever asked us for an arbitral tribunal. We could appoint a chairman to the board of railway commissioners in just about fifteen minutes, and I say now that we shall do so if either one of them wants an arbitral tribunal. I hope that is clear enough also.
That is another slander that has been going around in some of the Liberal press and repeated by some of the Liberal members. The hon. member for Shelburne-Yar-mouth unworthily took it up yesterday and cast it across the floor of the house. There has been no request by either railway for an arbitral tribunal, and the law is that the officers of one or the other must ask for an arbitral tribunal. We have been given no indication direct or indirect that they want one, and I say quite frankly, in my opinion neither one of them does, I do not say that one of them should not, but neither one of them has hinted that it wants an arbitral tribunal. When they want one, all they, 'have to do is to ask for it and they will get it quickly.
I have practically finished with the speech of the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth, but I wish to spend the remaining portion of my speech-and I hope I am getting toward the end of it, but I have had quite a few interruptions which have delayed me-in reviewing the record of this government. It is so well worth spending time on that I want to tell the country something about it. This government went through four years of economic storm such as no previous government of this country ewer went through, and I may add that our accomplishments did

The Budget-Mr. Manion
not wait, as has been implied by some of my hon. friends in their speeches, on the radio addresses of the Prime Minister in January. For five years courageous and aggressive administration has been carried on in this dominion by this government, and I intend to tabulate in just a sentence or two for each, the couple of dozen outstanding achievements of this government in the last five years:
1.	We spent about 8175,000,000 for relief, public works, assisting the provinces, the municipalities, the trans-Canada highway and the relief camps.
2.	We looked after 300,000 people and we are now looking after something like 150,000 in the drought areas in Saskatchewan. Further, an investigation has been instituted by the Department of Agriculture into that whole question.

Mr. Campbell saw marked evidence on the part of the Bennett government in its reciprocity proposals with the United States.

The Liberals have been opposed to everything ' that we have brought in of a progressive nature; they have either ridiculed it or opposed it as unconstitutional. Yet this session, although they ridicule and oppose it in argument, they always vote for it. The Liberal party in this house have been and are the party of reaction, the party of laissez-faire, the party of stand-patism, if they have any policy at all. No one has been able to see any sign of a policy as far as we can learn, no one has stated a policy for them except when my hon. and eloquent friend the member for Vancouver Centre

The Budget-Mr. Manion
(Mr. Mackenzie) gets up and waves his arms and tells us a few things. subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You will get a chance, and when you get it you will be pretty sick. They have offered no policy and as far as we know they have no policy except do-nothing. The people of this country know that they have a do-nothing policy, and when the time comes they will vote accordingly. We have been going through a world crisis for four years but apparently the Liberals in this house do not know it. In 1930 before they went out of office we spoke to them about the unemployment which was beginning then-and has increased since, I will say it so that they do not have to interject- due to world conditions, but their leaders took the attitude that there was no unemployment in this country. Then when the world crisis took place between 1929 and 1933 they have never admitted there was such a crisis. speechtext:
I said the world, I did not say Canada particularly-the whole world including Canada. We have suffered two great crises-probably I should say the world -in the last fifteen years; from 1914 to 1918, the war, and, rather strangely, four years again, the economic crisis, the depression, from 1929 to 1933. The latter has been almost as tragic to the world in general as was the war, except in our case we lost
60,000	of our young men who in the springtime of youth gave their lives for their country. They form a lost generation. Men from different parts of the country who would have been prominent in this house are among that lost generation, men who would probably be here instead of some of us had they come back. They were leaders at the front; they would have been leaders here. I have never forgotten the beautiful lines on the monument to the fallen in Glengarry county, which to my mind are among the finest words ever written about those who gave their lives in the war:
They shall not grow old as we who are left grow old;
Age shall not weary them nor the years condemn-
Those are the first two lines; I think I could remember the rest, but in any event they are a noble expression of our feelings. Yet I sometimes think that some of the men who stayed over there escaped tragedy which they might have encountered had they come back. But, sir, I want to point out that the tragedy from 1929 to 1933, was also a terrible trial to the young men throughout the world. I also want to point out that during the war there was a Liberal opposition in this house. My hon. friend from Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) and a number of hon. gentlemen opposite were members of the opposition at that time. But that Liberal opposition cooperated and assisted in every way. I was in the house in 1918, the last year of the war, and during that time the opposition assisted in every possible way. I do not understand why that is not the case to-day with hon. gentlemen like the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth, who had a magnificent record at the front, and I pay him all homage for that splendid record. At the front it was cooperation, assistance, playing the game and general leadership that were needed, and the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth exhibited all these to a marked degree together with my hon. friend from Quebec South (Mr. Power) and a number of other hon. members.

speechtext:
What was it I did?
The Budget-Mr. Manion

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
My hon. friend may deny it if lie cares to do so, but I should be afraid to deny it. However, these hon. gentlemen showed a willingness to cooperate and play the game over there, and I do not understand why they do not show a greater desire to play the game in times like these with a government that has had its own problems in a crisis such as that through which we have passed. I suppose it was too much to expect that the Liberal party would step right in and assist us to pilot the ship of state through the turbulent waters of the last few years, but I do submit that they ought to stop endeavouring to destroy the steering gear or blow holes in the bottom of the ship. That is what they have been doing. In some countries there is a crime called sabotage; workmen endeavour to destroy or cripple the plant and machinery of the institution in which they are employed. In Russia they shoot people for that sort of thing. But for five years in this house the Liberal party have been carrying on political sabotage against their own country. When they, and the rest of us, are old and grey, sir, if we are living, and a new generation has grown up which does not remember all the details of these tragic times, and when some of these young people ask my hon. friends opposite what they did in this parliament to help out during this economic crisis, if they tell the truth there is only one statement they can make, and that is to say, "We sat on the side lines and squawked."
Sir, Canada is on the march to better things. It will never be the same again, irrespective of the reactionary attitude of my hon. friends opposite or of any attitude on our part. Canada and the world are on the march. There is a great progressive movement under way but unfortunately our hon. friends opposite do not even recognize it. I admit with all humility that our program has been far from perfect, but it has been a program of progress and reform. Capitalism needs correction; no one realizes that more than I do. Those capitalists who do not realize it are short sighted; indeed they are blind. Our legislation, such as it is and with all its imperfections-and I admit them-is for the purpose of correcting the evils of capitalism. There are business men, I admit, who take the attitude that we should not be bringing in such legislation. Some hon. members here have defended that attitude of the business men, and I do not question their right to do so. But I think they are also blind, sir, because to my mind if those of us who believe in democracy and those of us who believe in the capitalist system, as I do, do not correct

these evils from within, then the day will come when these evils will be corrected in an appalling manner from without. Only one country has given up capitalism; that is Russia, and to my mind Russia has been a failure. Last year that country allowed five or six million people to starve, and over there if a man has an opinion of his own it is only too common for him to be sent off to Siberia or put up against a wall and shot. Therefore I submit that we must live under democratic capitalism if we are to go ahead. Capitalism is far from perfect, but it deserves much credit. It has been going on now for 150 or 200 years and during that time the population of the world, perhaps particularly in industrial countries, has been increasing by leaps and bounds. By a large, and in a general way, that population has been getting more comfort, more advantages in regard to health, better education and greater luxury than they would have known otherwise, and indeed than many of the medieval monarchs knew. It is true that some have been in want, but I do not think even those who have been in want-certainly in our own country where they have not been allowed to starve-would have willingly given up the adventure of life which they have experienced. They have had that adventure, and I do not think any individual would prefer to have missed the adventure, even though they have been through the trying times through which they have passed. I agree with Shakespeare, as I think we all do, when he says:
The weariest and most loathed worldly life
That age, ache, penury and imprisonment
Can lay on nature is a paradise
To what we fear of death.
So I say that at any rate, even those who have been in want have had the adventure of life. When days brighten, when business comes back throughout the world as it is coming back, once more they will get their chance. Mankind is groping for better things. Those of us who call ourselves leaders or are attempting to lead, my hon. friends opposite and those on this side as well, are groping for some remedy for the conditions with which we have been faced. We realize that there must be a fairer distribution of the wealth of the world. We realize that the problem of production has been solved, but that the fruits of that production must be more evenly distributed. We have not succeeded as yet. No country in the world-we are no exception-has succeeded in solving that problem of distribution. The young men of our country, as of other countries, must be given a chance to work; they must have an

Privilege-Mr. Brown
opportunity to attain their ambitions. They must be given, in simple language, a fair deal.
I say, sir, that the policies of this government and the statutes introduced by this government, imperfect though they may be, all are in line with that idea. The Conservative party in Canada is leading the Canadian people forward and upward in a progressive way, whereas hon. gentlemen opposite have been merely floating on the tide of discontent resulting from the unrest throughout the world, hoping to float back into power on that tide. But the people of this country are not blind; they see through the attitude of hon. gentlemen opposite, and when the time comes the people will treat them accordingly. Sir, Canada is leading the world out. All the indices, whether in regard to trade manufacturing, railway revenues, production, commodity prices or anything else, show that.
I see there is no time for another speaker to follow me before six, but I am practically finished-and I have lost the final page of my notes. Probably my hon. friends will say that is not important. For a moment or two I am going to quote some United States commentators who have expressed opinions upon Canada's condition. Before doing that, however, I should like to quote just the heading of the last daily bulletin issued by the bureau of statistics, dated March 22, just five days ago;
Weekly review of economic statistics. The business index was higher in February than in any other month for about four years.
Then I should like to quote from the Ottawa Morning Journal of November 15, 1934:
Toronto, November 14.-Officials of the Babson statistical organization at a "clients' conference" here to-day declared Canada had made the greatest recovery from the depression of any country.
Then here is a quotation from the business bulletin of the Cleveland Trust Company dated November 15. I will quote just the last paragraph:
The Canadian record in the reemployment of industrial workers is better than ours, although the difference is not- so striking as is that relating to production. In September Canadian employment in industry was 82 per cent as great as it was in 1929, while in -the United States it was only 70 per cent as great as the 1929 average. It is particularly noteworthy that in the first nine months of this year both industrial production and employment have made large net gains in Canada, and small net losses in the United States.
That is the view, sir, of men who look at us from the outside. I have mentioned Isaac Marcosson, who wrote an article which appeared not long ago in the Saturday Evening Post, and which I think was read by many of us, entitled North of the NRA. He loudly praised the work of -this country and of the Canadian people. Sir, it is something of which we may well be proud. I submit that when the time comes in the near future, within the next six months, that the people of Canada are given the opportunity to vote upon the activities and policies of this government, they will support 'it much more emphatically than they did in 1930. I know hon. members opposite -boast that they want an election. I remember well that they boasted to the same extent about victory in 1930, and they came back sitting to your left, Mr. Speaker. They will come back to your left again in 1935, just as surely as they are to your left to-day.
In closing may I say there have been two amendments, one offered by the hon. member for Shelbume-Yarmouth which is merely a negative of the whole budget resolution, and the other is an amendment by the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote) on behalf of the third party and which amendment at the present time I do not intend to discuss. The government cannot accept either amendment. Both involve a want of confidence in the government, and for that reason the government cannot and does not intend to accept them. I now urge the appeal, as I have in the past, that in the future hon. members opposite, even at this late stage of the session, give us more of that cooperation about which they boast and less of the criticism in which they so frequently indulge.

I did not wish to interrupt him when he was speaking, but I believe at this -time I should bring the matter to the attention of the house. Only a few days ago I heard a man describe as spicy reading the evidence coming from the Senate divorce committee. I hope the minister did not mean to imply that I was in the habit of telling stories spicy in that sense of the
